residents.name: Marananta
residents.variants: Mallananda; 摩羅難陀; 摩羅難陁
residents.nationality: UNCERTAIN (Western Regions/Serindia; some scholars argue Indian; came via Eastern Jin China)
residents.india_connection: If Indian (per some scholars, e.g., Lee Sang-ho 1960), the first Indian Buddhist to reach Korea; at minimum connected to Indian Buddhism via Central Asian monastic networks of the Jin period
residents.korea_connection: Arrived Baekje 384 (9th month, King Chimnyu's 1st year); received by the king; Buddhism 'began from this' (Samguk Sagi); temple built 385
residents.evidence: Samguk Sagi (sg_024r_0100_0030) and Samguk Yusa records; both mark 384 as the start of Baekje Buddhism
residents.significance: Traditional founder of Baekje Buddhism; earliest documented Buddhist arrival in Korean history

sources.citation: Samguk Sagi via National Institute of Korean History (sg_024r_0100_0030)
Samguk Yusa, Marananta entry (sy_003r_0010_0020_0010)
Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, '마라난타' (인도의 승려)

residents.name: Baedalta
residents.variants: 倍達多 (modern Sanskrit reconstruction not attested)
residents.india_connection: Indian monk who accompanied Gyeomik to Baekje in 531, carrying Sanskrit Abhidharma and Vinaya texts
residents.korea_connection: His arrival in Baekje (531) supported the establishment of the Vinaya school
residents.evidence: Korean Buddhist tradition (via Gyeomik narrative); encyclopedia entries on Baekje Vinaya
residents.significance: Attested Indian monk physically present in Korea; rare documented 6th-century India-to-Korea movement

sources.citation: Encyclopedia.com, 'Kyŏmik' (Baekje Vinaya)
Korean Wikipedia, '겸익'

residents.name: Dhyānabhadra
residents.variants: Jikong (指空); Shikong; Śūnyadiśya-Dhyānabhadra; Zhikong Chanxian
residents.india_connection: Born in Magadha (Indian royal family per tradition); ordained at Nalanda; famous in India before leaving
residents.korea_connection: Invited by King Ch'ungsuk (met at Mongol court); came to Goryeo 1326; founded Hoeamsa 1328 (reportedly modeled on Nalanda); influenced Korean Seon students incl. Naong Hyegeun and Muhak Chach'o; King Kongmin later sent his relics to Goryeo
residents.evidence: Hagiographical and scholastic records; temple foundation (Hoeamsa 1328); lineage transmission to Naong and Muhak
residents.significance: The last great Indian monk active in Korea; key figure in late-Goryeo Seon formation

sources.citation: Encyclopedia of Buddhism, 'Zhikong Chanxian'
Wikipedia, 'Dhyānabhadra'
Yangju Hoeamsa Museum (Yangju City), '지공선사' exhibit page
Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, '지공선사 부도 및 석등' (Hoeamsa Jigong stupa)
National Research Institute of Cultural Heritage, 금석문 DB: 양주 회암사지 지공선사 부도비 (stele text by Yi Saek)

residents.name: Buddhavara (Ven.)
residents.role: Buddhist monk; abbot of Bunhwangsa Temple India (분황사, Bodh Gaya); Chancellor of Bodh Gaya International College of Buddhist Studies; principal of Bodh Gaya International Meditation School; abbot at Sati Aramma (Kimhae)
residents.india_connection: Resident in Bodh Gaya leading Korean-led meditation training; signed academic-exchange MOU with University of Delhi (2026-04-23); honored in Korea as '인도 분황사 주지' (Beopbo, 2026-07-08)
residents.korea_connection: Foundational figure of Korean Buddhist institutions at Bodh Gaya; lecture circuits in Korea
residents.evidence: Delhi University MOU; multiple Korean Buddhist-press reports
residents.significance: Builder of the Korean Buddhist institutional bridgehead at Bodh Gaya

sources.citation: BTN (2026-04-23), 붓다가야 국제승가대학-델리대학 MOU

planned_pilgrims.name: Rabindranath Tagore
planned_pilgrims.role: Poet; novelist; playwright; essayist; educator; first Asian Nobel laureate in Literature (1913)
planned_pilgrims.india_connection: India's national poet; the central Indian figure of Korea's literary imagination in the colonial era
planned_pilgrims.korea_connection: Signed a 6-line English message dated 1929-03-28 (Tokyo) later known as 'The Lamp of the East' (동방의 등불), delivered at Yokohama departure for the Korean people; published in Dong-a Ilbo Apr 1929, translated by Chu Yo-han; planned a Korea lecture in June 1929 (cancelled for health); sent 'The Song of the Defeated' to Chin Hak-mun in 1916 (published in Ch'ŏngch'un Nov 1917); met Ch'oe Nam-sŏn and Chin Hak-mun in Tokyo/Yokohama 1916
planned_pilgrims.evidence: Dong-a Ilbo archival record; Hong Eun-taek's studies (2012, 2014); Choi Seong-woo's rhetorical analysis (2022); Kim Ujo (2014) in 인도연구; 2011 bust at Daehak-ro (gift of the Indian government)
planned_pilgrims.significance: The single most important Indian figure in Korean cultural memory of this period; his 'lamp' message became a national symbol of hope

sources.citation: Kyosu.net (2012-12-17), Tagore message transmission account (Hong Eun-taek)
JoongAng Ilbo 분수대 (2012-12-10), 'Reading between the lines on Tagore'

planned_pilgrims.name: Yi Yŏng-jae
planned_pilgrims.variants: Lee Young-jae; Yi Yeong-jae; dharma names Paekkwang (白光), Pŏmnan (梵鸞), Chongwŏn (宗圓)
planned_pilgrims.role: Monk (유학승); Buddhist reformer; first modern-era Korean monk to attempt an India pilgrimage
planned_pilgrims.india_connection: First modern-era Korean Buddhist pilgrimage attempt (1925): studied Sanskrit/Pali (Indian Philosophy) at Tokyo Imperial University; departed Yokohama 1925-11-09 for Ceylon (Sri Lanka) intending 2 years of study then an India pilgrimage; died in Ceylon 1927-10-12 before reaching India proper
planned_pilgrims.korea_connection: Colonial-era Buddhist reformer: '조선불교혁신론' (27 installments, Chosun Ilbo 1922); led the 조선불교동경유학생회 journal 금강저 (1924); travelogues 도석기/남국기/석란의 불교
planned_pilgrims.evidence: Ibulgyo 2021-02-03 biography (한국불교 격동 100년 series); Dong-A Ilbo 1927-10-27 obituary; KCI ART003193373; Beopbo series entry
planned_pilgrims.significance: Pioneer of modern Korea-India Buddhist engagement: first Korean monk in centuries to set out for India; his vow and writings mark the start of the modern pilgrimage era

sources.citation: Ibulgyo (불교신문) 2021-02-03, 이성수: '[한국불교 격동 100년] <1> 근대 최초 인도 순례한 이영재 스님' - full biography: born 1900 Cheongju; ordained 1918 Beopjusa; Nihon Univ 1920-23; Tokyo Imperial Univ Indian Philosophy (Sanskrit/Pali); departed Yokohama 1925-11-09 on Hakusan Maru; Ceylon Dec 1925; died 1927-10-12 in Ceylon aged 28; wrote 도석기/남국기/석란의 불교; drew taegeukgi for Mahabodhi Society Vesak in Kandy; Dong-A Ilbo 1927-10-27 obituary
Beopbo (법보신문) series entry: '⑦ 이영재 스님(1900~1927)' - 1924 Nihon Univ grad; 1925 Sri Lanka via India pilgrimage; died en route
KCI ART003193373: '이영재(李英宰, 1900~1927)의 남아시아 기행 탐구' - academic study of his Ceylon journey and pilgrimage writings
Ibulgyo (불교신문) 2026-04-15: '독일학자 찐머만, 근대 구법승 이영재 스님 재조명' - German scholar Zimmermann re-examines Lee Young-jae as first modern Korean Buddhist pilgrim

events.significance: Earliest documented enshrinement of an Indian master's relics in Korea; material anchor of the Jikong lineage at the Nalanda-modeled Hoeamsa

sources.citation: Dongguk University Buddhist Culture Portal (불교문화포털, buddhaland.dongguk.edu, KBDI0001421) '지공' entry: on King Kongmin's order (1370) a stupa enshrining Jikong's relics was built at Hoeamsa, supervised by Naong, declaring Naong's succession of Jikong

Hyunbul News 2017-01-26: '지공·나옹… 재점화된 禪宗' - Jikong's representative disciples: Naong (Kongmin's preceptor), Baegun Gyeonghan (Jikji author), Muhak Chach'o (T'aejo's preceptor), Ch'ukwŏn Chich'ŏn; revival of studies on Jikong's Seon lineage

events.title: Return of Hoeamsa relics (Jikong/Naong + Buddha relics) from Boston MFA
events.description: Relics of Dhyānabhadra (Jikong) and Naong, enshrined with Buddha relics (Shakyamuni, Kashyapa, Dipankara) that Jikong brought from India, were returned to Korea from the Boston Museum of Fine Arts (illegally removed during the colonial era; acquired by the MFA 1939; return agreed 2023-24): delivered 2024-04-16, arrived in Korea 04-18, relocation rite at Jogye's Buddhist History & Culture Memorial Hall 04-19, re-enshrined at Hoeamsa 2024-05-19
events.significance: Modern completion of the 14th-century relic legacy: relics of Indian provenance (Buddha's relics carried from India by the Indian master Jikong) physically returned to the temple he founded

sources.citation: Hankook Ilbo 2024-04-17: Hoeamsa sarira return finalized - relics of Jikong/Naong plus Buddha relics (brought from India by Jikong) illegally removed in the colonial era, acquired by Boston MFA 1939; return agreed after the 2023 US state visit; delivered 2024-04-16, Korea arrival 04-18, relocation rite at Jogye 04-19, re-enshrinement at Hoeamsa 2024-05-19
Ibulgyo 2024: '회암사 3여래2조사 사리' - Jogye Order had a separate sarira reliquary made for the returned Hoeamsa relics

events.title: Wang ocheonchukguk jeon first public display at National Museum of Korea
events.description: The BnF's Dunhuang manuscript of Hyecho's Wang ocheonchukguk jeon (往五天竺國傳) - the sole surviving 8th-century record of India by a Silla monk - was loaned to the National Museum of Korea for the '실크로드와 둔황: 혜초와 함께 하는 서역기행' special exhibition (18 Dec 2010 - 3 Apr 2011; manuscript on display until 17 Mar 2011 per the BnF's 3-month loan limit): the manuscript's first public display anywhere since Pelliot's 1908 Dunhuang discovery; a second BnF loan followed for the NMK exhibition Dec 2019 - Apr 2020
events.significance: World-first public display of Korea's oldest travel record of India; made Hyecho's 8th-century India pilgrimage tangible for the Korean public and scholars

sources.citation: National Museum of Korea press archive 2010-06-29: '혜초의 『왕오천축국전』 한국에 온다' - BnF review board approved (17 Jun 2010) loaning the Wang ocheonchukguk jeon manuscript for the '실크로드와 둔황' exhibition (18 Dec 2010 - 3 Apr 2011); first public display of the manuscript since Pelliot's 1908 Dunhuang discovery
KBS News 2010-12-17: '1283년만에 한국 온 왕오천축국전' - the BnF manuscript arrived in Korea for the NMK '실크로드와 둔황' exhibition; first public display in 1,283 years

Hani (한겨레) 2019-10-19: '혜초의 왕오천축국전 고국 찾아온다' - second BnF loan approved (17 Oct 2019) for the NMK exhibition Dec 2019 - Apr 2020; manuscript 358.6cm scroll, 227 lines, 5,893 characters; Pelliot discovery 1908; Takakusu Junjiro's 1915 Silla attribution; Ch'oe Nam-sŏn's 1943 Korean introduction
